\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}
\label{ch:ta-asking-age}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone's age in both the casual possessive shape and the formal dative-plus-become shape, and answer with my own.}

Complete TA-C19-checkpoint, the chapter's closing checkpoint: ask an age casually and formally and answer in the formal shape, place vayathu in Sanskrit vayas, say what \ta{◌ி} and \ta{ச} do, find \ta{◌ே} in \ta{பேசு}, then write \ta{றி}, \ta{சரி} and \ta{◌ே} from sound.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ta{உனக்கு} \ta{எத்தனை} \ta{வயது} … (unakku ettanai …)}{உனக்கு எத்தனை வயது … (unakku ettanai …)}]{\ta{உனக்கு} \ta{எத்தனை} \ta{வயது} \ta{ஆகிறது}? (unakku ettanai vayathu aakirathu?) — Tamil actually has BOTH shapes}

\label{lesson:TA-C19-vayathu}



\begin{quote}
Same Sanskrit word one more time — but be careful here: Tamil isn't locked into just one of the two grammatical shapes you've now seen. It has both, in different registers.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வயது} — the same Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}vigor/age\textquotedblright{} word, a fourth time}
\textbf{\ta{வயது}} (\emph{vayathu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{age}\textquotedblright{} — the same Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{वयस्}} (\emph{vayas}, \textquotedblleft{}age, vigor,\textquotedblright{} PIE cousin of Latin \textbf{vīs}) you've now met four times across Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam, and Tamil. All four Dravidian languages borrowed this exact Sanskrit word for \textquotedblleft{}age\textquotedblright{} — none of them built a native alternative for this particular concept, the way they did for so many others.

\textbf{In the family, and next door}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
Kannada & \ka{ನಿನ್ನ} \ka{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \ka{ಎಷ್ಟು}? (\emph{ninna vayassu eṣṭu?}) \\
Telugu & \te{నీ} \te{వయసెంత}? (\emph{nī vayasenta}) \\
Malayalam & \ml{നിങ്ങൾക്ക്} \ml{എത്ര} \ml{വയസ്സുണ്ട്}? (\emph{niṅṅaḷkkŭ etra vayassuṇṭŭ?}) \\
English & how old are you? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}vayathu\textquotedblright{} — age — then the whole formal question, \textquotedblleft{}unakku ettanai vayathu aakirathu?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Connect:} Sanskrit \emph{vayas} · Tamil \emph{vayathu} · Latin \emph{vīs}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is Tamil's \textbf{\ta{வயது}} the same Sanskrit word borrowed by all four Dravidian languages here? (\textbf{Yes} — none built a native alternative for this concept.) What did \emph{vayas} originally include besides age? (\textbf{Vigor}.) Next: choose between Tamil's casual possessive and formal dative-plus-become shapes.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ta{உன்} \ta{வயசு} \ta{என்ன}? … (un vayasu enna? …)}{உன் வயசு என்ன? … (un vayasu enna? …)}]{Your age what? / To you how many years becomes?}

\label{lesson:TA-C19-age-register-grammar}



\begin{quote}
Tamil did not choose one age construction. Register selects between two shapes already visible elsewhere in the family.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Casual possessive}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{உன்} \ta{வயசு} \ta{என்ன}?} — \textquotedblleft{}your age what?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Casual speech uses a plain possessive with no dative and no verb, like Kannada and Telugu.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Formal dative plus \textquotedblleft{}become\textquotedblright{}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{உனக்கு} \ta{எத்தனை} \ta{வயது} \ta{ஆகிறது}?} — \textquotedblleft{}to you how many years is becoming?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எனக்கு} \ta{இருபது} \ta{வயது} \ta{ஆகிறது}.} — \textquotedblleft{}to me twenty years is becoming.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Formal/written Tamil uses the dative experiencer plus \textbf{\ta{ஆகிறது}} (\emph{aakirathu}, \textquotedblleft{}is becoming,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{aaku}). Malayalam uses a similar dative shape but chooses \textquotedblleft{}exists\textquotedblright{} instead.

Do not compress these into \textquotedblleft{}Tamil's one grammar.\textquotedblright{} Both live in the language; setting and register choose between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}un vayasu enna?\textquotedblright{} — casual
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}unakku ettanai vayathu aakirathu?\textquotedblright{} — formal
  \item \emph{Answer:} \textquotedblleft{}enakku irupathu vayathu aakirathu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape is casual? (\textbf{Possessive}: \textquotedblleft{}your age what?\textquotedblright{}) Which is formal? (\textbf{Dative + aakirathu}, \textquotedblleft{}become.\textquotedblright{}) Does Malayalam use the same verb? (\textbf{No} — it uses \textquotedblleft{}exists.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ta{ி} (i sign)}{ி (i sign)}]{\ta{ி} — the first vowel sign}

\label{lesson:TA-S09-i-sign}



\begin{quote}
Not a letter this time — a mark that changes the letter under it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ி}}
A consonant carries \emph{a}. To make it carry a different vowel you add a \textbf{sign} — and the sign replaces the built-in vowel rather than sitting beside it.

The i-sign is a hook written above and to the right. \ta{ற} is \emph{ṟa}; \ta{றி} is \textbf{ṟi}.

Where it sits: a hook written above and to the right of the consonant

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{ி}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/TA-S09-i-sign-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ta{ி} is written, stroke by stroke}

And with that: \ta{நன்றி}.

\begin{quote}
\ta{ந} + \ta{ன} + \ta{்} + \ta{ற} + \ta{ி}
\end{quote}

\emph{Thank you} — the second word you can write.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} the mark on a letter you already know
  \item \emph{Say it:} the letter's sound with the mark, then without it
  \item \emph{Write it:} the whole word above, one mark at a time
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does a vowel sign add a vowel or replace one? (\textbf{Replace} — the built-in \emph{a} is gone.) What is \ta{ற} with an i-sign? (\textbf{ṟi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ta{சரி} (sari)}{சரி (sari)}]{\ta{சரி} — one letter, several sounds}

\label{lesson:TA-W07-write-sari}



\begin{quote}
You have seen \textbf{\ta{க}} cover \emph{k}, \emph{g} and a soft \emph{h} depending on where it sits. Here is the same economy on a second letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ச} and \ta{ர}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/TA-W07-write-sari-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ta{சரி} is written, part by part, stroke by stroke}

\textbf{\ta{ச}} is written once and does the work English splits between \textbf{s}, \textbf{ch} and \textbf{j}. Position picks which:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{sound} \\
\midrule
starting a word & \emph{s} or \emph{ch} \\
between vowels & softened \\
after a nasal, as in \textbf{\ta{ஞ்ச}} & \emph{j} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is exactly the pattern \textbf{\ta{க}} showed — \emph{k} at the start, \emph{g} after a nasal, a soft \emph{h} between vowels. One letter per position of the mouth, and context fills in the rest.

\textbf{\ta{ர}} is \emph{ra}, with its built-in \emph{a}. It is the other of Tamil's \textbf{two} \emph{r}-letters, alongside the \textbf{\ta{ற}} you met in \textbf{\ta{நன்றி}}.

\begin{quote}
Read both letters here. The strip writes \ta{ச}, \ta{ர} and then the \ta{ி} sign, numbered movement by movement, with each source beneath it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: build the word}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ச}} & \emph{sa} here & this lesson \\
\textbf{\ta{ரி}} & \emph{ri} — \ta{ர} with the \ta{ி} sign & the sign from \textbf{\ta{நன்றி}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ச} · \ta{ரி} $\to$ \ta{சரி}}
\end{quote}

Two pieces, and both parts are things you already hold: a consonant, and the vowel sign you first hooked onto \textbf{\ta{ற}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ச}} — then \textbf{\ta{சரி}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ta{ரி}} and \textbf{\ta{லை}} — the \ta{ி} sign follows its letter, the \ta{ை} sign precedes it
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ta{ஆம்}} and \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} again, from memory — yes and no, the two you will reach for most
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{சரி}}. Which English sounds does \textbf{\ta{ச}} cover on its own? (\emph{\textbf{s}} or \emph{\textbf{ch}} at the start, softened between vowels, \emph{\textbf{j}} after a nasal.) How many \emph{r}-letters does Tamil keep? (\textbf{Two} — \ta{ர} and \ta{ற}.) In \textbf{\ta{லை}}, which side of the \ta{ல} does the ai sign sit on? (\textbf{The left}.) And why does \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} open with \textbf{\ta{இ}} rather than a sign? (\textbf{It starts on a vowel}.) Next: the numbers eleven to twenty.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ta{ே} (ē)}{ே (ē)}]{\ta{◌ே} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TA-S123-vowel-sign-ee}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ta{த} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{◌ே}}
\textbf{\ta{◌ே}} — \emph{ē}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ē}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ta{◌ே} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}} \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ta{பேசு}} \emph{pēsu} — to speak
  \item \textbf{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{பேசுகிறேன்}} \emph{nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ} — I speak Tamil
  \item \textbf{\ta{வேலை} \ta{செய்}} \emph{vēlai sey} — to work (lit. \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{◌ே} — follow the numbered strip}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/TA-S123-vowel-sign-ee-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ta{ே} is written, stroke by stroke}

Follow the numbered strip: start where movement 1 begins, and let each panel show you the next movement before your pen makes it. Then write \ta{◌ே} yourself — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
The strip shows \textbf{where to start the character and which way to travel}, in one attested order. That is taught with real variation from school to school, so the strip names its source beneath it: treat it as a sound way in, not the only one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ta{◌ே} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ta{பேசு}  ·  \ta{வணக்கம்}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{◌ே} three times, saying \emph{ē} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ta{◌ே} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{◌ே}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ē} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 19 checkpoint — two ways to ask an age, and \ta{சரி} from sound}

\label{lesson:TA-C19-checkpoint}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new here. The age question in both its shapes first, then a vowel sign, a word and one more sign on the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the age question}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the casual question, to a friend
  \item \emph{Say it:} the formal question, to someone you would address with care
  \item \emph{Answer:} in the formal shape, giving twenty as the age
\end{itemize}

(\emph{Un vayasu enna?} — \emph{Unakku ettanai vayathu aakirathu?} — \emph{Enakku irupathu vayathu aakirathu.})

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Where does \emph{vayathu} come from? (Sanskrit \emph{vayas}, \textquotedblleft{}age, vigor\textquotedblright{}, which all four Dravidian languages here borrowed.)
  \item Which shape uses the dative and \emph{aakirathu}, \textquotedblleft{}becomes\textquotedblright{}? (The formal one; the casual one is a plain possessive with no verb.)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — \ta{◌ி}, \ta{ச} and \ta{◌ே}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Does \textbf{\ta{◌ி}} add a vowel or replace one? (It replaces the built-in \emph{a}: \textbf{\ta{ற}} is \emph{ṟa}, \textbf{\ta{றி}} is \emph{ṟi}.)
  \item Which sounds does \textbf{\ta{ச}} cover on its own? (\emph{s} or \emph{ch} at the start of a word, softened between vowels, \emph{j} after a nasal.)
  \item Which two pieces build \textbf{\ta{சரி}}? (\textbf{\ta{ச}} · \textbf{\ta{ரி}}: \ta{ர} carrying the i-sign.)
  \item In \textbf{\ta{பேசு}}, \emph{pēsu}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}, which mark gives the first consonant its \emph{ē}? (\textbf{\ta{◌ே}}.)
\end{itemize}

\emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{சரி}} and \textbf{\ta{பேசு}} aloud, and point to the \ta{◌ே}

\subsection*{Writing — from sound}
\emph{Cover:} the Script block above, so no model stays in view

\emph{Write it:} \emph{ṟi}, then \emph{sari}, \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Write it:} the sign that turns a consonant's \emph{a} into \emph{ē}

\emph{Check:} against the key — \textbf{\ta{றி}}, \textbf{\ta{சரி}}, \textbf{\ta{◌ே}}

\emph{Write it:} one repaired shape, then stop

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A friend asks your age, then an elder does. Which shape does each one use? (The possessive for the friend; the dative with \emph{aakirathu} for the elder.) That is the chapter: one borrowed word, two grammars, and \emph{okay} written from sound.

Next chapter: the numbers eleven to twenty.
\end{tcolorbox}
